turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. ____. Nice to meet you. Well, I suppose what brought me in is that... I keep getting up when I'm supposed to be sitting down. Like in staff meetings or even just at dinner when everyone else is seated. 

I've been teaching secondary school for over thirty years now, mostly history, and you know how teenagers are these days—they can't sit still for five minutes without looking at their phones. I had this one student last term, lovely boy, but constantly distracted by everything outside the window. They really need to fix the landscaping out by the science wing, to be honest, the bushes are completely overgrown and it blocks the light. 

But, um, what was I saying? Oh, right, my meetings. Yes, I'll be in a meeting and I'll just suddenly feel the need to go refill my coffee, or I'll think I have to check a handout right that very second, or I'll just walk to the back of the room. Even though nothing is really urgent at all! I just end up on my feet. I actually brought my own coffee today because the stuff in the staff lounge is just dreadful, it's this cheap dark roast that gives me terrible heartburn... anyway, yes, I just can't seem to stay in my chair.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they keep getting up in situations where they are expected to remain seated, such as during staff meetings or at dinner.

turns.doctor_question: Were you like this as a child too?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yes. Actually, I was just going through some old boxes in the attic last month because my husband wanted to clear out space for his model trains. He's been collecting them since the eighties, O-gauge mostly, and they take up half the loft... but anyway, I found my old primary school report cards in one of the boxes. My mother had saved them all in this lovely floral binder. 

And every single one of them said the exact same thing—that I was a bright girl, but I just could not stay in my seat or wait my turn. My mother used to joke about it all the time. She'd say I wore a literal path in the floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old! 

Which is funny when you think about it, because kids today don't even use those crank pencil sharpeners anymore. It's all mechanical pencils now. The clicking noise those mechanical ones make drives me absolutely up the wall during exams, just click-click-click across the whole room... but, um... what was I saying? Oh, right, my childhood. Yes, always on the move, even back then.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by going off on tangents about her husband's model trains and mechanical pencils, eventually losing her train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states that her childhood report cards noted she 'could not stay in my seat.'
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes her childhood self as being 'always on the move.'
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient mentions that her report cards indicated she could not 'wait my turn.'

turns.doctor_question: Do you also often have trouble paying close attention to details or making careless mistakes?
turns.patient_response:
Careless mistakes? No, I wouldn't say so. I'm actually quite particular about details, especially when I'm marking exams. You really have to be, don't you? Especially with history. If you get the dates wrong, the whole timeline just falls to pieces. Take the Tudor period, for instance. I always tell my students you simply cannot mix up Henry VIII's wives. I have this lovely little rhyme I teach them, though half of them just look it up on Wikipedia anyway. 

Wikipedia is such a menace sometimes, isn't it? I mean, it's brilliant for a quick search, but anyone can edit it. My husband was looking up something about his model trains on there just last Tuesday—the Hornby ones, specifically—and he found a glaring error about the manufacturing year of a particular locomotive. He was so cross about it, he actually tried to figure out how to edit the page himself. He spent about three hours clicking around the computer with his reading glasses slipping down his nose, muttering to himself about historical accuracy... 

But, um... sorry, what was the question? Oh! Careless mistakes. Right. No, no, I don't really do that. I'm usually very sharp with details.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies making careless mistakes and states she is very sharp with details.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by her own unrelated thoughts about Wikipedia and her husband's trains, causing her to forget the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, going on a long, rambling tangent before returning to the question.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often lose things you need, like keys, papers, or your glasses?
turns.patient_response:
Lose things? No, no, I'm actually quite organized. I always put my keys in the little ceramic bowl by the front door. It's a lovely bowl, actually, my daughter painted it for me when she was in university. She went to art school in Cornwall, beautiful place, right by the sea. The light there is just extraordinary, painters have been going there for over a century just for the natural light. We used to visit her on bank holidays and eat fish and chips on the pier, though you have to be so careful with the seagulls. I swear they're the size of small dogs down there, and they'll take a chip right out of your hand if you aren't paying attention. One actually swooped down and knocked my husband's glasses right off his face once! They fell straight into the water, and we had to spend the rest of the afternoon trying to find an optometrist open on a Sunday... 

Oh, goodness, what were we talking about? Losing things! Right. No, my memory for where I put my things is perfectly fine. I keep track of everything quite well.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by their own unrelated thoughts about a bowl, art school, and seagulls, temporarily forgetting the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, going on a long, unprompted tangent before finally answering the question.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly denies having trouble with organization, stating, 'I'm actually quite organized.'
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly denies losing things, stating they keep track of everything quite well and their memory for where they put things is perfectly fine.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often interrupt other people before they’ve finished speaking?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, interrupt? Yes, I suppose I do that quite a bit, actually. Especially in group discussions. At our book club or during the curriculum meetings at school, I often just jump right in before someone has even finished their thought. It's just that the response is already right there in my head, and I blurt it out before I can even stop myself! 

I did it just last week at book club, actually. We were reading that new historical fiction novel about the Mitford sisters. Fascinating family, really. Did you know Unity Mitford actually went to Germany and became quite close with Hitler? It's just extraordinary to think about. The author took some creative liberties, of course, which always annoys me a bit as a history teacher. If you're going to write historical fiction, you should at least get the timeline right. Like I was saying earlier about the Tudors—accuracy matters! Anyway, Brenda, our club president—lovely woman, makes the most incredible lemon drizzle cake—she was right in the middle of making a point about Nancy Mitford's writing style, and I just completely talked over her to correct a historical date. I felt terrible afterward, but the thought was just sitting there on my tongue and it had to come out. 

Brenda's lemon drizzle cake, though... I really must get the recipe from her. She uses actual lemons from her conservatory, not that bottled juice nonsense. My husband tried growing lemons once, but he gave up when the aphids got to them. He said it was too much fuss and went back to his model trains... 

But, um... oh! Interrupting. Yes. I do tend to blurt things out before people are finished speaking.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states that they tend to 'blurt things out' and 'blurt it out before I can even stop myself' when others are speaking.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient confirms they often interrupt others, jumping in before people have finished their thoughts during group discussions and talking over them.

turns.doctor_question: Before these difficulties started in childhood, or did they only begin later in adulthood?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, it's definitely been since I was a little girl. My mother used to joke that I wore a path in the floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old! I just couldn't sit still. And my report cards always said the same thing—"bright girl, but cannot stay in her seat or wait her turn." 

My old primary school was one of those beautiful Victorian buildings, you know the ones with the incredibly high windows so the children couldn't look out and get distracted? Not that it stopped me, of course. I was always finding a reason to hop up. The headmistress there, Mrs. Gable, she was terrifying. Wore these tweed skirts that looked like they could stand up on their own, and she had a stare that could freeze water. But even she couldn't keep me in my chair. 

Actually, the school was converted into luxury flats a few years ago. Such a shame, really, losing all that history. My husband and I went to an open house for one of the flats just out of curiosity, and they had completely stripped out the original wainscoting! I was furious. I mean, why buy a historical building if you're just going to turn it into a sterile white box? The estate agent didn't know what to do with me when I started lecturing him about the architectural significance of the era... 

But, um... right. Childhood! Yes, the report cards and the pencil sharpener. It's always been there, right from the start.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes that high windows designed to prevent children from getting distracted did not stop her from being distracted.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient recalls childhood report cards stating she could not stay in her seat and mentions she was always finding reasons to get up.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly states her childhood report cards noted she could not wait her turn.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find it hard to sustain your attention when you need to focus on reading, listening, or doing paperwork?
turns.patient_response:
Sustain my attention? No, not really. I mean, I read quite a lot, actually. I can sit with a book for hours, especially if it's a good biography. I was just reading one about Queen Victoria's early years. Fascinating, really. She was so young when she took the throne, just eighteen! Can you imagine being given an entire empire to run at eighteen? When my daughter was eighteen, she could barely remember to take the bins out, let alone rule half the world. 

Though, to be fair, Victoria had Lord Melbourne to help her. They had such an interesting dynamic, didn't they? Some historians think he was a father figure, but others suggest it was a bit more... complicated. I actually watched a documentary about it on BBC Four the other night. BBC Four has the best documentaries, don't you think? None of that flashy editing they do on the main channels now. Just proper historians talking in dusty libraries. I love a dusty library. There's a second-hand bookshop in our village that smells exactly like old paper and Earl Grey tea. The owner, Mr. Henderson, he's been there since the eighties. He always saves the new history arrivals for me...

Wait, what was the question? Oh, sustaining attention. Yes. No, I don't have any trouble with that. I can focus just fine on my reading and my marking for school.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a lengthy, rambling response, going off on tangents about Queen Victoria, documentaries, and a local bookshop.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly denies having trouble sustaining attention, stating they can focus just fine on reading and school marking.

turns.doctor_question: Have these difficulties caused problems for you at work, at home, or in your relationships?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, actually. It has started to cause a bit of a fuss lately. Mostly at work and in the community, you know? People are just... losing patience with me. In the staff meetings at school, or at the book club I mentioned. I just talk over them or jump in, and I can see their faces tighten up. I always leave feeling so embarrassed instead of feeling connected to anyone. 

It's a terrible feeling, really. Leaving book club and realizing you've alienated Brenda again. And Brenda is such a pillar of the community. She organizes the summer fete every year, and it’s a massive undertaking. The tombola alone takes weeks of planning. Last year, I volunteered to run the hook-a-duck stall, but the water leaked everywhere because my husband bought a cheap paddling pool from the discount shop instead of a proper one. I told him, I said, "Arthur, you can't cut corners on a paddling pool," but he insisted it would be fine. He’s always doing that, trying to save a few pennies here and there. He bought these awful off-brand digestive biscuits once, and they tasted like cardboard. You just can't mess with a classic digestive, especially when you're dipping it in tea. The structural integrity is completely different...

But, yes. The embarrassment. It’s definitely affecting my relationships at work and with my friends because they get so frustrated with me in meetings.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a lengthy, rambling response that goes far off-topic, demonstrating excessive talking.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly admits to talking over people and jumping into conversations during meetings and book club.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits marked tangentiality, drifting from the book club to a summer fete, a paddling pool, her husband, and eventually the structural integrity of digestive biscuits.
